Q: Get value from dataframe transformation with regex A:

You're only removing spaces from the column, not the other special characters. Try

regex_replace('/[ \[\]"]', "", col('nom_prenom_detenteur'))

Q: Test the randomness of a black box that outputs random 64-bit floats A:

As this is an interview question, I think the interviewers are looking to assess in two ways:

  1. Ability to understand what the requirements of the problem really are.
  2. Ability to think of some code that would address those requirements.

This could be a really good interview question in certain settings, especially if the interviewer were willing to prompt the candidate with questions as and when necessary.

In terms of understanding the requirements of the question, it helps if you know that this is a really difficult problem, witness the Diehard tests mentioned in pjs's answer. Fundamentally I think a candidate would need to demonstrate appreciation of two things:

(a) The overall distribution of the numbers should match the desired distribution (I'm assuming it is uniform in this case, but as @pjs points out in comments this assumption should be made explicit).

(b) Each number drawn should be independent from the previous numbers drawn.

With half an hour to code something up in a phone interview, you can't go very far. If I were answering this question I would try to suggest something like:

(a) To test the distribution, come up with a set of equal-sized bins for the floating point numbers, and count the numbers that fall into each bin. Plot a histogram and eyeball it (plotting the data is always a good idea). To extend this, you could use a chi-squared test, as described in amit's answer.

However, as discussed in the comments, and here

The main problem with chi squared test is the choice of number and size of the intervals. Although rules of thumb can help produce good results, there is no panacea for all kinds of applications.

To this end, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test can be used. The idea behind this test is that a plot of the ordered data should be a good fit against the perfect ordered data (known as the cumulative distribution). For a uniform distribution the perfect ordered data is a straight line: you expect the 10th percentile of the data to be 10% of the way through the range, the 20th to be 20% of the way through the range and so on. So, programmatically, you could sort the data, plot it against the ideal value and you should get a straight line. There is also a formal, quantitative statistical test you can apply, which is based on the differences between the actual and ideal values.

(b) To test independence, there are multiple approaches. Autocorrelation at various time lags is one fairly obvious one: to what extent is the value at time t similar to the value at time t+1, for example. The runs test is another nice one: you convert all the numbers into 1 or 0 depending on whether they fall above or below the median, and then the distribution of the length of runs can be used to construct a statistical test. The runs test can also be used to test for runs in one direction or another, as described here and here (this might be more useful in your case). Both of these have fairly straightforward implementations so long as you have the formulas to hand!

Apart from the diehard tests, other good sources discussing random number generators include here and here.

Q: Pipe to/from the clipboard in a Bash script A:

Users of Windows terminal and XTerm:

Windows Terminal is now fully ANSI code compatible. Meaning that it conforms to both new and classic VT100 control character definitions. A particular subset of those as known as Operating System Commands (OSC) and one specific command thereunder allows you manipulate the selection and clipboard data buffers (plural).

From the Xterm Escape Sequences manual, we can read the following:

In other words, we can manipulate:

  • clipboard
  • primary (clipboard)
  • secondary (clipboard)
  • select, and
  • cut buffers 0-7

Example-1

If you are using Windows Terminal to ssh into a Linux host, you can use the following little (bash) script to copy a file to the clipboard of the windows host:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# clipfile.sh - send a file to the Windows Terminal clipboard
# Original psot was using: ${1:?} - An empty message
printf $'\e]52;c;%s\a' "$(base64 ${1:?[ERROR] No file was was provided!})"

The explanation here is:

  • \e] = ESC ] = 0x9D = OSC (Operating System Command)
    Starts a control string for the operating system to use, terminated by ST.

  • 52; = Use OSC 52 to Manipulate Selection Data

  • c;<data> = Add <data> string to the clipboard.
    It has to be a string, which is why we have to base64 encode it to preserve control and EOL characters.)

  • \a = BEL = 0x07 - That is actually the terminal "bell" character.
    but here it is used as the ST (String Terminator) of OSC.

  • $(...) - open a subshell

  • base64 <data> - Convert <data> to base64 (ASCII)

  • ${1:?Error!} - Is a Bashism for saying:
    "If there is an argument/file ($1) use that as input, otherwise display the "Error!" message.

A nice modification could be to include using piped data or wait for manual input.

Example-2

Here are some other variants found in nature..

printf $'\e]52;c;%s\a' "$(base64 <<<'hello world')"
printf "\033]52;c;%s\007" "$(base64 | tr -d '\n')"

Example-3 (Full Solution)

Here is a full solution allowing both pipes and filename with error checking.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# zclip.sh - send a file to the Windows Terminal clipboard
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# Description:
#   Copy to clipboard using OSC 52, and "c".
#   Other available options are: [c, p, q, s, 0 .. 7]
#   For [ clipboard, primary, secondary, select, or cut-buffers (0-7) ].
#
# Other variants:
#   printf $'\e]52;c;%s\a' "$(base64 <<<'hello world')"
#   printf "\033]52;c;%s\007" "$(base64 | tr -d '\n')"
#   printf $'\e]52;c;%s\a' "$(base64 ${1:?Error: No file was provided})"
#
# Notes:
#   - pipe data can be retrieved with $(cat -1), but can't be retrieved again after.
#     pipe_data=$(cat -)
#
# References:
#   [1] https://stackoverflow.com/a/76171051/1147688
#   [2] https://invisible-island.net/xterm/ctlseqs/ctlseqs.html#h3-Operating-System-Commands
#   [3] https://ansi.tools/lookup
#   [4] https://linuxsimply.com/bash-scripting-tutorial/redirection-and-piping/piping/read-from-pipe/
#
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
rline () { TT="$1"; echo -e "\e[1;31m${TT}\e[0m"; }

if [ "$#" -ne 0 ]; then
    # We got a filename
    DATA="$1"
    if [ -f "$DATA" ]; then
        printf $'\e]52;c;%s\a' "$(base64 ${DATA:?[ERROR] No file was was provided!})"
    else
        rline "\n[ERROR] file doesn't exist!\n"
    fi
else
    if [[ -p /dev/stdin ]]; then
        # We got pipe data
        DATA=$(base64 -)
        printf $'\e]52;c;%s\a' "${DATA:?[ERROR] base64 did not like the pipe data!}"
    else
        rline "\nUsage: [<piped-data>] | zcip.sh [<filename>]\n"
    fi
fi

# END

Tested and uploaded here from Debian via Windows.

Does this work with other terminal and console programs?

Q: Why is my title bar not showing up in my Tkinter messagebox? A:

If "title" is not working, you can put your title in the "message" column and your message in the "detail" column for a similar effect. This works better on Mac because of the software.

messagebox.showwarning(message='Oops!', detail="Please don't leave any boxes empty.")

Q: Why can adding logging make a Python race condition disappear? A:

Printing a newline is going to force a chapter 2 write() syscall, which is going to be a big thing for scheduling.

Prefer to log to memory. For example, by appending strings to a list.

At which point you have several choices to make. One list, or a list per thread? Are you willing to make a time.time() syscall to include a timestamp in each log entry? Are you willing to maintain a single global sequence number, which will appear in each log entry? You probably want to protect that counter with a mutex, don’t you?

Consider having multiple threads append messages to a single Queue. It will produce correct behavior, but of course it will have the side effect of altering the thread scheduling.

Prefer to use thread safe data structures, such as a Queue, when you author a new application. That is, design races out of your solution.

Many people are fond of approaching such tasks as a message passing problem. For example, you might create threads that are kafka producers and consumers.

Interpreter 3.14 lets you drop the GIL.

Interpreter 3.15 offers improved "no GIL" support. At that point it's mostly OS thread support that controls the scheduling, with minimal involvement from the interpreter. Similar to linking against a "debug" malloc library, you have the option of linking against a "debug" scheduler, which deliberately tries to produce odd interleavings, so we explore a larger portion of the feasible state space.

Suppose you wish to better understand the behavior of a big chunk of racy legacy code, while still managing to provoke those race conditions. Issuing write() requests and other syscalls will disturb the schedule and perhaps hide the race. One approach is to let the app code run for a "long" time, longer than a scheduling quantum, and to make "few" syscalls. So we might append these final two lines:

    for i in range(100_000):
        value = counter
        counter = value + 1
        if i % 1000 == 0:
            print(f"{i=}")

You probably want to include the thread number in such log entries. And you might possibly want the if to trigger only for a single thread.

Indiscriminate print() debugging can be effective for a small single-threaded function, but when working with a large legacy code base you likely want to be more selective about debugs. You might already have a theory in mind that you want to test, and so a sensible if condition could ask whether the abs() difference between two counters ever exceeds some constant, perhaps a hundred. Or perhaps you're trying to understand when the race happens, so the if might trigger just when 2nd counter exceeds the 1st one, optionally calling breakpoint() for that event.

what is a reliable way to reproduce ... these timing-dependent bugs

I understand the desire to follow the usual game plan:

  1. report the bug
  2. reproduce it
  3. write a "red" failing unit test
  4. author a fix
  5. see the test turn "green"

But the trouble with races is they tend to be a poor match for that reliable reproduction step, something that automated unit tests really need. So as soon as I understand there's a race happening, usually the first thing I will do is pepper the code with mutexes and such, to kill the race. Now, that may also kill performance. But at that point you have a reliable "green" unit test plus a "performance stinks" bug report, which you can turn the crank on. Remove one mutex at a time from your app until you see acceptable performance. If removing the mutex turns your test "red", then you know you've gone one step too far and should back out that edit.
